correctness.rationale: Summing the masses with t=theta+1 and c=theta²/t gives F(z)=c(t+1-z)/(t-z)² and G=pi+(1-pi)F. For p_0>0 the Taylor coefficients are (2 t^(-n)-sum r_j^(-n))/n, where r_j are the finite numerator roots. When 0<pi<1, the quadratic in s=t-z is pi s²+(1-pi)c(s+1); both roots have negative real part, so the corresponding z roots have modulus >t. At pi=0 the single root is t+1; pi=1 gives the point mass. In the negative branch set q=(1-pi)c/(-pi); the positive root of s²-q(s+1)=0 rises strictly from t to infinity, putting one z root rho down from zero through -t, and the other eta stays >t. The equation at rho=-t is q=4t²/(2t+1), giving the displayed pi_* and its strictly positive distance from pi_min. For rho<=-t even coefficients are bounded below by (t^(-n)-eta^(-n))/n>0 and odds are positive as well. For -t<rho<0, negative even coefficients eventually dominate. Real iid roots with p_0>0 cannot have a negative part (all copies could be negative); they must have an atom at 0 and then lie on the integer lattice, since the other copies can all be zero. At truncation, the shifted PGF has a single numerator zero t(theta+3)/(theta+2)>t, so its log coefficients are positive and summable and G=zH gives explicit fractional-shift real roots. Integer roots at truncation cannot exist for order m>1 since the minimal possible summed integer count would be m times the least supported count, not 1. The boundary coefficients remain strictly positive at every fixed degree, so continuity at fixed positive p_0 provides the arbitrarily late obstruction; no finite enumeration is needed. For theta=1 the right-hand boundary roots are -2 and 14/5, and at pi=-1/3 I get p_0=1/6, p_1=1/3, p_2=5/24 and lambda_2=-3/4. The first two raw moments are 2 and 22/3, so the overdispersion example also checks. Frozen checker read, not executed; the mass recurrence it uses follows from G'=G(log G)' and is independent as a finite coefficient computation.

value.rationale: For an established model whose defining flexibility is zero inflation and deflation, the two notions of divisibility give genuinely different phase diagrams, and the isolated ordinary-ID law cannot be read from the coefficient test for positive zero mass. The result both supplies the exact admissible region for a jump interpretation and explains why finite coefficient screening or overdispersion can falsely suggest it. No empirical jump mechanism or inference guarantee follows.
